title: A midday pause
hookLine: many traditions stop at noon: the Angelus, dhuhr prayer
tomorrow: two psalms disagree about whose food this is. who's right?

cards: Lunch can be a sandwich eaten over a keyboard. In the book of Daniel, the middle of the day is dangerous.
Officials who resent Daniel talk King Darius into signing a law: for thirty days, no one may pray to any god or man except the king. Whoever does goes to the lions. And here is the odd detail.
Daniel hears the law is signed, goes home, and kneels at his windows, wide open toward Jerusalem.

teach.b: Here's the verse: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."
The puzzle solves itself in the last words: as he did aforetime. He isn't staging a protest. The windows were already open toward Jerusalem; the knees already bent three times a day.

teach.h: THE LAW CHANGED. HIS DAY DIDN'T.
teach.b: The law changed. His day didn't. That's the teaching.

In the Hebrew Bible, prayer is tied to set times of day, and a psalm names them: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." The day is stitched together by fixed hours, and noon is one of the stitches.
The pattern runs on among the neighbors, each in its own way: the Angelus bell at noon in Catholic parishes that keep it, and dhuhr, the Muslim prayer just after the sun passes its height.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the psalm puts evening first, and some readers hear an echo of Genesis, where a day runs from evening: "the evening and the morning were the first day."

teach.h: A FIXED STITCH IN THE DAY.
teach.b: And Daniel? The lions' mouths are shut, and he comes out unharmed.
Notice what noon was for him. Not a break from the day, but a turn toward something larger, at a time that came whether he felt like it or not.

how: Jewish prayer keeps fixed times of day, Muslims pray dhuhr after midday as one of the daily prayers, and in some Catholic parishes a bell rings the Angelus at noon; on this path a noon pause is borrowed with its source named.

o: one fixed stop at midday, turned toward something larger
a short nap after eating to get through the afternoon
a long lunch break taken far away from your desk

p: the king who signed the law
evening, and morning, and at noon

s: Daniel opened his windows to defy the king in public
the text says he prayed 'as he did aforetime': the habit came first, and the law didn't change it.
the psalm names noon as one of the set times of prayer
"Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray."
in the story, the lions wound Daniel but he survives
the lions' mouths are shut, and he comes out unharmed.

games.q: your dad keeps a short prayer at noon, but this week he's on a long road trip with no quiet place. what fits Daniel's story?
o: keep the set time anyway, even briefly: the hour matters more than the setting.
skip it until he's home; a pause only counts somewhere quiet.
save it all for the evening and do the day's prayers at once.
games.why: Daniel kept his times 'as he did aforetime', even under a ban. the fixed hour held his day together.

practice: Choose a direction to face when noon comes, a window or a patch of sky, the way Daniel faced Jerusalem. Practice it once now: turn toward it, stand still, and let a few slow breaths be the whole pause.
A line of thanks fits here, as Daniel gave thanks, or simply the stillness.

wordCard.voice: A midday pause: one fixed stop in the middle of the day. For Daniel, a window open toward Jerusalem, as he did aforetime.

orig.note: Hebrew: noon, the word in Psalm 55:17 (55:18 in Hebrew Bibles).

carryVoice: Here's your line: noon, kept the way Daniel kept it, as he did aforetime. Back tomorrow.
